title: Controlling Decarburization in Steel: A Coupled Reaction-Diffusion Model for Annealing Processes

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hot-dip galvanizing lines comprise multiple coupled thermo-chemical and fluid-dynamical process steps, including annealing, zinc bath interactions, and gas-jet wiping. While previous studies have modelled zinc bath phenomena [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ]  and coating-thickness control during wiping, [ 7 , 8 ]  the present work addresses predictive modelling of surface decarburization during annealing. The controlled decarburization during heat treatment in an annealing furnace is crucial for attaining the mechanical properties and deep-drawing capabilities required for automotive applications. [ 9 ]

In the existing literature, various modelling approaches have been proposed to predict decarburization rates. Early analytical models utilized error functions to estimate the depth of decarburization. [ 10 , 11 ]  These models, however, often overestimate the decarburization depth, necessitating the adjustment of diffusion coefficients as scaled parameters to align the predictions with the observed data. A more accurate representation of the decarburization process can be achieved by considering the maximum solubility of carbon in ferrite rather than relying solely on scaled diffusion coefficients. [ 12 , 13 ]

One limitation of these analytical models is their assumption of constant temperature and diffusion coefficients, as well as the neglect of varying atmospheric conditions encountered during processing. To address this, a numerical finite difference model was developed that connects surface reactions with carbon diffusion, offering a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between these two processes. [ 14 ]  However, this model focussed exclusively on the diffusion of carbon in ferrite, which led to predictions of high decarburization depths.

Some methodologies have explicitly addressed the interface between ferrite and austenite by employing a differential volume method that accounts for the interface movement during phase transitions, [ 15 ]  however, without taking varying atmosphere conditions into account. This approach assumes a distinct boundary between ferrite and austenite, which may not accurately reflect the real-world conditions. Research has demonstrated that during the heating cycle, austenite grains can form around carbide particles, leading to a more complex microstructure characterized by interconnected ferrite regions. [ 16 ]  Further advancements in modelling have incorporated an effective carbon diffusion coefficient that varies with the actual phase fractions of ferrite and austenite present in the steel, based on the equilibrium phase diagram, [ 17 ]  eliminating the need for an accurate representation of the concentration jump in carbon at the ferrite–austenite interface. This approach is comparable to Reference  18 .

In this study, we developed a decarburization model that couples the surface reaction and the 1-D diffusion of carbon in steel in a manner both physically grounded and computationally efficient. A promising strategy is to use thermodynamic equilibrium phase fractions from the Fe–C system to describe the distribution of ferrite and austenite as a function of local temperature and composition and to represent multi-phase diffusion through an effective diffusion coefficient that transitions smoothly between ferritic and austenitic diffusivities. The model parameters were determined using a differential evolution algorithm by fitting the predicted carbon concentration profile with Glow Discharge Optical Emission Spectroscopy (GDOES) measurements, ensuring that the model accurately reflected the decarburization behaviour of steel during the annealing process.

This model aims to provide a more accurate prediction of decarburization by considering the complex interactions between the gas atmosphere, temperature, and phase fractions, ultimately enhancing the understanding of the decarburization process.

sections.heading: Glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy (GDOES)
paragraphs: The carbon concentration profile was determined by Glow Discharge Optical Emission Spectroscopy (GDOES) using a Radio-Frequency (RF) source.

Prior to analysis, the specimen was mechanically polished and cleaned with ethanol. The sample was mounted flush against the anode to ensure stable plasma conditions. Measurements were conducted under argon atmosphere in RF mode to prevent the formation of insulating layers on the cathode surface.

Sputtering was performed at constant discharge voltage, resulting in the emission of characteristic radiation from excited atoms and ions. The emitted light was detected by a polychromator equipped with photomultiplier detectors. Carbon was quantified using the emission line at 165 nm.
The instrumental parameters were as follows:
Discharge type: RF mode
Argon pressure: 300 Pa
Voltage: 700 V
Anode diameter: 4 mm
Pre-sputtering time: 0 s

Elemental concentrations were calculated using calibration factors obtained from certified reference materials. The depth scale was derived from the sputtering time and the measured crater depth, yielding a carbon concentration profile with micrometer-scale resolution.

sections.heading: Model Optimization
Decarburization Model Calibration and Validation
paragraphs: The comparison between the measured GDOES carbon concentration profile (blue points) and the optimized model (black line) is shown in Figure  8 . The measured carbon concentration profile represents the mean and standard deviation of the measurement across steel samples taken from the start, the middle and the end of the coil. A good agreement between the measured and the modelled carbon concentration profile is achieved with an in-sample SMAPE of 10.6 pct.

sections.heading: Data-Driven Analysis
Process Insights: Temporal Evolution of the Carbon Profile
paragraphs: The proposed model is a fast and applicable model to predict the decarburization in steels. However, there are some limitations: One is that oxidation is not considered, which might influence the decarburization reaction, especially at higher dew points, when a continuous oxide layer forms at the surface and the direct contact between water vapour and carbon is reduced, as discussed in Section  II–A . Another point is that the actual phase change kinetics are only indirectly considered by presuming a phase-transition parameter that affects the carbon diffusion coefficient. Thus, the model parameters should be fitted with a similar temperature curve as in the process because the time-dependent phase changes are implicitly included in the model parameters.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this work, a coupled surface-reaction 1-D carbon diffusion model for the calculation of the decarburization during annealing was introduced. The focus was put on a physically sound and computationally efficient approach. A practical framework to fit the required model parameters to annealing experiments was shown. A leave-one-out cross-validation was conducted to analyse the robustness of the model and its predictive performance. The main benefit of the model is its ability to substantially reduce the number of required annealing trials by enabling rapid calculation of carbon profiles for a wide range of process conditions. Furthermore, the model is capable of giving insights in the temporal evolution of the carbon concentration profile during non-isothermal annealing. It was shown that the main decarburization occurs during the heat-up period.
